title: Atwemo
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Diamonds of nutmeg dough pulled through their own slits and fried at 365 degrees — if they sink and stay there, the oil is not hot enough.
longDesc: Atwemo are crisp twisted biscuits, rolled thin, cut into inch-long diamonds, slit in the centre and pulled through themselves to twist. Four cups of flour with two teaspoons of baking powder, half a cup of sugar, half a teaspoon of nutmeg, half a cup of margarine, an egg and three quarters of a cup of milk. The oil goes to about 365 degrees, and the test is the best in the collection: if the oil is not hot enough they fall to the bottom and stay there; if it is too hot they bounce up immediately and brown before they are cooked through. They should be quite golden — perhaps a little browner than you think at first.
ingredients: 1/2 cup margarine — 1 cube. In Ghana they use margarine; butter gives a slightly different texture
3/4 cup milk — in Ghana, half evaporated milk and half water
// Variations: instead of nutmeg, use grated orange rind, caraway or aniseed, or leave out the vanilla.
equipment: Deep fryer or deep heavy pan
steps: Sift the flour, salt, nutmeg and baking powder together in a large bowl.
Rub or cut the margarine into the sifted ingredients with a pastry blender or your hands.
Add the sugar and mix with a spoon.
Beat the egg slightly with a fork, add the milk and vanilla, and mix together.

Add the liquid to the flour mixture and mix well, then knead lightly but not enough to make it tough. Add a little more flour if it is sticky, a little more milk if it seems too dry and will not hold together.
Divide the dough into 4 equal parts.
Roll each out to between 1/8 and 1/4 inch — thinner for harder, crispier atwemo.
Cut into strips about 1/2 inch wide, then cut diagonally into diamonds about an inch long.
Cut a slit in the centre of each diamond.
Pick up a diamond, push one end through the slit and pull it all the way through to twist it.
// If you do not pull the dough all the way through you get what her children called 'birds' — they taste fine.
Fill a deep fryer or pan no more than half full with oil and heat to about 365 degrees Fahrenheit.
Carefully but quickly slip a couple of dozen atwemo in one by one. Do not drop them and splatter the oil.
If they fall to the bottom and stay there the oil is not hot enough. If they bounce up immediately and brown before cooking through, it is too hot.
Stir frequently and turn them so they brown on both sides. They should be quite golden — perhaps a little browner than you think at first. It takes only a few minutes a batch.
Remove with the slotted spoon into a paper-towel-lined colander to cool.
Store covered in an airtight container.
chefTips: The sink-or-bounce test is the best oil cue in this collection and needs no thermometer: sinking and staying down means too cool; bouncing straight up and browning fast means too hot.
Quite golden, perhaps a little browner than you think at first. Under-browned atwemo are soft rather than crisp.
Roll thin for crisp. Her own preference is the thin end of the eighth-to-quarter-inch range.
Never fill the pan more than half full. It bubbles up hard when the dough goes in.
Knead lightly. Over-kneading these makes them tough, and the same applies when you re-roll the scraps.
Skip the twisting if you like and just cut triangles — but cook the untwisted ones separately, because the cooking times vary a bit.
They freeze beautifully, so a large batch is worth it. Margarine rather than butter is what they use in Ghana and it does change the texture.
commonMistakes: Frying at the wrong temperature and ignoring the sink-or-bounce signal.
Pulling the diamond only part way through, giving 'birds'.
Filling the pan more than half with oil.
Mixing twisted and untwisted shapes in one batch.
servedWith: Ice cream or a fruit salad
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #21: Atwemo (twisted cakes)', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Friday 16 October 2009. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 3:33 PM', timestamped 2009-10-16T15:33:00-05:00. Yield: NONE PRINTED. Quantities, oil temperature, thickness, cut dimensions and doneness cues all confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

A RETRIEVAL NOTE: the permalink was initially refused, and the verbatim pass was obtained from the blog's October 2009 archive index page, which carried the full post text. The two passes are therefore the archive rendering and the permalink rendering of the same post.

Ingredients exactly as printed: '4 cups flour'; '1/2 teaspoon salt'; '2 teaspoons baking powder'; '1/2 cup sugar'; '1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg'; '1/2 cup margarine (1 cube) [in Ghana they use margarine; if you substitute butter the dough will have a slightly different texture]'; '1 egg'; '3/4 cup milk (in Ghana I make it with half evaporated milk and half water)'; '1 teaspoon vanilla flavoring (I always use real vanilla)'; 'vegetable oil for deepfrying (I like canola)'. The flour is printed as plain '4 cups flour' with no type and no sifted or unsifted qualifier, even though the method directs sifting.

THE OIL CUE, verbatim and the reason this entry is worth having: 'If the oil is not hot enough the atwemo will fall to the bottom of the pan and stay there. If it is too hot they will bounce up immediately and brown before they are cooked all the way through.' A two-sided observable test, not a thermometer reading.

THE FRY-DONENESS CUE, verbatim: 'They should be quite golden when they are ready; perhaps a little browner than you think at first. It will only take a few minutes to cook each batch.' NO NUMERIC FRY TIME is printed — doneness is by colour.
THE DOUGH CUE, verbatim: 'Add a little more flour if it is sticky, a little more milk if it seems too dry and will not hold together.'

Dimensions as printed: roll 'to between 1/8 and 1/4 inch'; strips 'about 1/2 inch wide'; diamonds 'about an inch long'; dough divided into '4 equal parts'; oil 'never more than half full'; '365 degrees Farenheit' — spelling as printed. 'margerine' is also printed thus in the method. Neither is corrected.
NO REST OR RISE STEP EXISTS in this recipe. It is chemically leavened with baking powder, so the collection's fermentation rule does not apply.

THE REMARK WORTH KEEPING, verbatim: 'If you do not pull the dough all the way through you will end up with what my children used to call "birds." These will taste fine, but it's better to learn to twist the dough properly.'

VARIATIONS as printed: 'instead of nutmeg, use grated orange rind, caraway or aniseed, or leave out the vanilla.' And on keeping: 'Atwemo freeze beautifully well if you want to make a large batch. They work equally well as a snack or a dessert alone or served with ice cream or a fruit salad.'

THREE CLAIMS REJECTED as single-pass summariser artefacts, recorded so they are not mistaken for source text: that the recipe 'can be halved' (no yield or halving advice appears in the verbatim pass); that the atwemo 'can be frozen unbaked' (the verbatim text refers to freezing finished, fried atwemo); and that atwemo are framed on this page as holiday foods 'similar to Nigerian chinchin' (no such sentence appears — the chinchin and puff-puff comparison belongs to the bofrot post at GHA114). None of the three is published.
NO YIELD is printed. The twelve servings above is an editorial reading of four cups of flour.
storage: 2 weeks in an airtight container. They freeze beautifully.
reheating: A low oven briefly to re-crisp.
healthBenefits: Egg and milk contribute complete protein.
Portion-controlled by nature, since they are small.
No preservatives, and the sugar is modest for a fried sweet.
culturalNote: Atwemo are the Ghanaian tin-of-biscuits snack, made in big batches at Christmas and Easter and kept for visitors, and the twist is the whole craft of them. The detail that half-pulled ones become 'birds' is the sort of thing only a cook who taught children to make them would write down.
